subject: Geography
description: Monsoon, seasons, climate zones, El Nino impact

questions.stem: India's CLIMATE is characterised mainly as:

options.option_text: Tropical monsoon (with seasonal reversal)
Temperate (like Europe, year-round even)
Polar (very cold all year long)
Desert (uniformly arid everywhere)

questions.explanation: INDIA'S CLIMATE: 'TROPICAL MONSOON' — defined by SEASONAL REVERSAL of winds + rains. KEY FEATURE: SW MONSOON (June-Sept) brings ~75% of annual rainfall; NE MONSOON (Oct-Dec, mainly TN, AP). FOUR SEASONS: WINTER (Dec-Feb, cool dry), SUMMER (March-May, hot dry), SW MONSOON (June-Sept, wet), POST-MONSOON / autumn (Oct-Nov, humid hot). CLIMATE VARIATIONS: tropical (Kerala, TN, coast), subtropical (UP, Punjab), semi-arid (Rajasthan), desert (Thar), Himalayan alpine. WORLD'S WETTEST PLACE: Mawsynram (Meghalaya, ~11,872 mm/year); Cherrapunji nearby. THAR: ~150 mm/year. MASSIVE diversity reflects continental size + Himalayas + monsoon dynamics. INSIGHT — India's monsoon is the world's most prominent monsoon system, affects ~1.4 billion people.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: SW MONSOON enters India through which route first?

options.option_text: Kerala coast (~1 June onwards)
Mumbai coast (~10-15 June)
Andaman Islands (mid-May)
Delhi (late June onwards)

questions.explanation: SW MONSOON OFFICIAL ARRIVAL: KERALA coast around 1 JUNE (sometimes earlier). Spreads progressively NORTH-EAST. ANDAMAN-NICOBAR sees rains EARLIER (~mid-May) but monsoon's mainland arrival is dated by KERALA. PROGRESSION: Kerala (June 1) → Mumbai (~June 10) → Bay of Bengal arm reaches Bengal/NE India by June 5; covers Delhi by ~June 29; covers ALL of India by ~July 8. RETREAT begins September from NW. TWO BRANCHES of SW MONSOON: ARABIAN SEA branch (hits Western Ghats; 80%+ rainfall on western slope; rain shadow on Deccan east); BAY OF BENGAL branch (hits Bangladesh + NE; deflected by Himalayas → west along plain → reaches Delhi, Punjab). MAWSYNRAM (Meghalaya) gets HEAVIEST rains due to BoB branch + funnelling effect. IMD (India Meteorological Department) forecasts monsoon onset.

questions.stem: EL NIÑO typically affects India by:

options.option_text: Weakening monsoon → drought tendency
Strengthening monsoon → flooding
No effect on Indian climate at all
Causing extreme cold winters in north

questions.explanation: EL NIÑO = warming of EASTERN PACIFIC equatorial waters (off Peru). DISRUPTS WALKER CIRCULATION → weakens SW monsoon over India → DROUGHT TENDENCY. BUT not absolute — some El Niño years had normal/above monsoon (depends on combined factors). NOTABLE Indian DROUGHTS in El Niño years: 1899, 1972, 1987, 2002, 2009, 2015. LA NIÑA = OPPOSITE (cooling) → STRONGER monsoon, often abundant rains. Recent strong La Niña: 2020-22 (good monsoons). INDIAN OCEAN DIPOLE (IOD) = parallel cycle in Indian Ocean (West vs East Indian Ocean SST difference); +ve IOD → favorable monsoon, −ve → adverse. ENSO + IOD together determine Indian monsoon strength. IMD provides PROBABILISTIC FORECASTS based on these. CLIMATE CHANGE making monsoon more ERRATIC — same total rain but in concentrated bursts → more floods + droughts.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: World's WETTEST place by annual rainfall is:

options.option_text: Mawsynram (Meghalaya, India ~11,872 mm/yr)
Cherrapunji (Meghalaya, ~11,777 mm/yr)
Tutunendo (Colombia, S America)
Mt. Waialeale (Hawaii, USA) too

questions.explanation: MAWSYNRAM — Khasi Hills, Meghalaya. Annual avg rainfall ~11,872 mm (~12 m!). Held GUINNESS WORLD RECORD for highest avg annual rainfall. CHERRAPUNJI / SOHRA (15 km away) — close 2nd at ~11,777 mm; held earlier record for wettest. WHY: BoB monsoon + funnel-shape Khasi hills → orographic uplift; clouds dump rain. India also has driest places (Jaisalmer, Leh ~50-150 mm). LEH (Ladakh) — extreme cold-desert. RAJASTHAN-Thar — ~150-300 mm. Mt WAIALEALE (Kauai, Hawaii) — 12,300 mm by some reports. TUTUNENDO (Colombia) — claims of 13,000+ mm. CLIMBED RECORDS sometimes contested — geographic sampling issues. INDIA's varied rainfall reflects monsoon dynamics + topography. WORLD's RAINIEST DAY (24-hr rainfall): Cilaos, Réunion (1966) ~1825 mm. WORLD's RAINIEST MINUTE: Unionville, Maryland — 31 mm in 1 min (1956).

questions.stem: WESTERN DISTURBANCES bring WINTER rainfall to which region of India?

options.option_text: North India (esp. Punjab, Haryana, J&K)
South India (Kerala, TN coastal)
NE India (Assam, Meghalaya etc.)
Eastern coast (Odisha, AP, Bay)

questions.explanation: WESTERN DISTURBANCES (WDs) — extra-tropical CYCLONES originating in MEDITERRANEAN sea, travelling east via Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan into NORTH INDIA. Bring WINTER RAINS (Dec-Feb) + SNOWFALL in Himalayas. KEY for: rabi crops (esp. WHEAT in Punjab/Haryana — winter rain very useful); skiing in Himachal/Kashmir. WITHOUT WDs, North India would be much drier. NUMBER: ~8 in winter; some bring intense rain/snow. EXAMPLES: SNOW in Shimla, Manali, Sonmarg in Jan-Feb directly from WDs. NE MONSOON brings Oct-Dec rains to TN + AP coast (very different system). MAVTHA = local term for surprise WD-rain in Punjab/Haryana. WD ALSO causes COLD WAVES in N India when intense (clear skies + radiation cooling at night). Recent: WDs slightly weakened in some years due to climate change effects.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: TROPIC OF CANCER passes through approximately how many Indian STATES?

options.option_text: 8 states (Gujarat to Mizoram E-W)
5 states (only central India)
12 states (entire India coverage)
3 states (only some south)

questions.explanation: TROPIC OF CANCER (23.5°N latitude) — passes through 8 Indian states (W to E): GUJARAT, RAJASTHAN, MADHYA PRADESH, CHHATTISGARH, JHARKHAND, WEST BENGAL, TRIPURA, MIZORAM. Divides India into TROPICAL SOUTH (warmer year-round) + SUBTROPICAL NORTH (more seasonal extremes). EQUATOR (0°) — passes through Indonesia, Brazil, Congo, Kenya, Ecuador, Colombia, Gabon, Maldives — NOT India (closest Indian point: Indira Point, Great Nicobar at 6.74°N). TROPIC OF CAPRICORN (23.5°S) — through Australia, Chile, Brazil, Madagascar, S Africa. INTERESTING: India straddles tropical + subtropical zones → extremely diverse climate. ANTARCTIC + ARCTIC CIRCLES (66.5° each) — well outside India. KEY GEOGRAPHIC FACT: India lies between 8°4'N + 37°6'N latitudes; 68°7'E + 97°25'E longitudes. STANDARD TIME: IST = UTC+5:30 (based on 82.5°E, passing through Mirzapur, UP).

questions.stem: RAINFALL on the EASTERN SIDE of Western Ghats is LOW because of:

options.option_text: Rain-shadow effect (windward side gets rain)
Lack of monsoon entry from west (option here)
Cold ocean currents nearby coast
Insufficient mountain height for rain

questions.explanation: RAIN SHADOW: WESTERN GHATS face Arabian Sea (W) → SW monsoon hits, rises, cools, RAINS on WINDWARD (western) side (Konkan, Malabar coast — heavy rainfall, ~3000+ mm). Air now DRY descends on LEEWARD (eastern) side → rainshadow → DECCAN PLATEAU is dry (~600-1000 mm). Same effect: Mahabaleshwar (Western Ghat top) ~6000 mm, Pune (~30 km east) ~700 mm. Other RAIN SHADOW examples: TIBET (north of Himalayas — only ~100 mm; Himalayas rain on south side); LEH (north of Pir Panjal); KIBO of Kilimanjaro. ATACAMA DESERT (Chile) = world's driest, in rain shadow of Andes. WHY DECCAN ROCKY → over millennia, less rain + erosion produced PENINSULAR PLATEAU character. KEY GEOGRAPHIC INSIGHT — same monsoon, different rain due to TOPOGRAPHY.

questions.stem: The hot, dry, westerly wind known as 'Loo' blows during summer afternoons across which geographical region of India?

options.option_text: Coastal Karnataka and Kerala — regions of high humidity
The semi-arid plains of Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana and UP
The plateau regions of Marathwada and Vidarbha in Maharashtra
The Brahmaputra valley in Assam and the Meghalaya hills

questions.explanation: The Loo is a hot, dry north-westerly surface wind that blows over the Indo-Gangetic plains (Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, UP, Bihar) in May–June, sometimes pushing temperatures beyond 45 °C. Kerala and Karnataka are coastal with high humidity — Loo-type conditions cannot persist there. The Deccan plateau and Brahmaputra valley experience entirely different wind regimes.

questions.stem: Pre-monsoon rains locally called 'Mango Showers' assist mango ripening in April–May. These showers are primarily associated with which region?

options.option_text: Vidarbha plains and the cotton-growing belt of Maharashtra
The arid and semi-arid districts of western Rajasthan
Kerala and coastal Karnataka along the Western Ghats region
The flood-prone plains of Assam and the Brahmaputra delta

questions.explanation: Mango showers are localised convective pre-monsoon rains in April–May over Kerala and coastal Karnataka, triggered as the overhead sun shifts northward and sea-surface temperatures warm, fuelling afternoon convection. West Bengal's equivalent pre-monsoon storms are separately named 'Kalbaisakhi'; Rajasthan is too arid for significant convective pre-monsoon rains.

questions.stem: Tamil Nadu receives the bulk of its annual rainfall during October–December, when most of peninsular India is dry. What is the primary source and mechanism for this rainfall?

options.option_text: The southwest monsoon's Arabian Sea branch retreating southward
The northeast monsoon winds picking up moisture from the Bay of Bengal
Western disturbances tracking eastward from the Mediterranean Sea
Convective rainfall generated by intense surface heating during November

questions.explanation: Tamil Nadu lies in the rain-shadow of the Western Ghats for the SW monsoon, so it receives little June–September rainfall. During October–December, northeast trade winds blow onshore across the Coromandel coast after picking up substantial moisture from the Bay of Bengal — this constitutes the northeast (retreating) monsoon. Western disturbances (Option C) affect only northwest India and weaken long before reaching Tamil Nadu.

questions.stem: A 'positive Indian Ocean Dipole' (positive IOD) is associated with above-normal Indian monsoon rainfall. What does a positive IOD specifically describe in terms of sea-surface temperatures?

options.option_text: Warmer sea surface in the eastern Indian Ocean near Indonesia
Cooler waters near Indonesia and anomalously warm waters off East Africa
Uniform 1–2 °C warming of the entire Indian Ocean surface layer
Warmer Bay of Bengal and cooler Arabian Sea than seasonal averages

questions.explanation: Positive IOD = anomalously warm SST in the western Indian Ocean (near East Africa and the Arabian Sea) plus anomalously cool SST in the eastern Indian Ocean (near Indonesia/Sumatra). This gradient strengthens atmospheric convection over the western basin, pushing extra moisture toward India. Option A describes a negative IOD — warmer eastern IO — which suppresses Indian monsoon rainfall and often co-occurs with El Niño.

questions.stem: The 'break in monsoon' — a spell of little or no rainfall over the Gangetic plains during the monsoon season — is climatologically linked to which positional shift?

options.option_text: The monsoon trough shifts southward toward the Deccan and the western coast
The monsoon trough shifts northward, lying along or near the Himalayas
The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) migrates westward into Arabia
The Bay of Bengal branch weakens as cyclonic activity in it diminishes

questions.explanation: During a 'break,' the monsoon trough — the east-west low-pressure axis that normally runs across central India — migrates northward to lie close to the Himalayan foothills. This moves convergence away from the Gangetic plains (causing a dry spell there) while delivering intense orographic rainfall to the foothills. Option A is the opposite: a southward trough shift would intensify rainfall over central India, not suppress it.

questions.stem: 'Kalbaisakhi' (Nor'westers) are violent pre-monsoon thunderstorm squalls that damage crops in West Bengal and Assam each April–May. Which combination of conditions best explains their origin?

options.option_text: Western disturbances from the Mediterranean meeting cold Himalayan airflow
Intense surface heating triggers convective instability, met by moist Bay of Bengal inflow
Cyclonic circulation from the Arabian Sea intensifying along the Eastern Ghats
Cold northerly winds descending from the Himalayas colliding with warm Bay air

questions.explanation: Kalbaisakhi form when extreme daytime heating of the Bengal–Bihar plains in April–May creates steep lapse rates and strong surface convergence (convective instability). Moisture-laden southerly winds from the Bay of Bengal flow in simultaneously; where hot, dry northwesterly surface air collides with this moist influx, explosive convection produces hail, lightning and destructive squalls. Western disturbances (Option A) are extratropical cyclones that bring winter rain to northwest India — they are entirely unrelated to Kalbaisakhi.

questions.stem: The Mascarene High, a semi-permanent subtropical anticyclone in the southern Indian Ocean, plays a foundational role in India's southwest monsoon. What is this role?

options.option_text: It acts as a heat source intensifying the low-pressure cell over the Thar Desert
It drives the cross-equatorial airflow that Coriolis force converts into SW monsoon winds
It generates the subtropical westerly jet stream steering depressions into northwest India
It suppresses cyclone formation in the Bay of Bengal during the pre-monsoon season

questions.explanation: The Mascarene High (centred near 30°S) pushes air northward along its western flank. As these southerly winds cross the equator into the Northern Hemisphere, the Coriolis effect deflects them rightward (eastward), producing the characteristic southwesterly flow that constitutes the SW Monsoon. The Thar Desert thermal low (Option A) results from land-surface heating — not from the Mascarene High. The subtropical westerly jet stream (Option C) is a separate upper-tropospheric feature over the Himalayas whose seasonal withdrawal helps the monsoon advance.
